  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
# Rajesh

Rajesh Patel had spent thirty-two years handling explosives for the city's bomb disposal unit. He had walked toward devices that would have killed ordinary men without hesitation. He had trained himself to move with absolute precision under conditions that would shatter most people's nerve. Discipline, control, and the ability to compartmentalize were the architecture of his professional identity. Then, in the spring of 2019, his eight-year-old daughter Priya developed a fever that would not break.

What began as a routine illness escalated over four days into something that landed her in the pediatric intensive care unit with meningitis. Rajesh remembered the moment the attending physician had said the word—the way it seemed to hollow out the room. He remembered Priya's small body in the hospital bed, her skin mottled, her breathing labored. He remembered the needles. Endless needles. An IV line that had to be reinserted three times because her veins kept collapsing. A lumbar puncture that Priya had screamed through while Rajesh stood at the foot of the bed, forbidden from holding her, watching her suffering and unable to stop it. He had defused bombs. He had talked down suicidal individuals. He had controlled his fear response in situations where hesitation meant death. But in that room, with the antiseptic smell coating the back of his throat and the beeping monitors creating a rhythm of dread, he had felt something break inside him—a recognition that his competence, his training, his decades of discipline meant absolutely nothing here.

Priya had survived. After ten days, the antibiotics worked. She came home. But Rajesh did not come home with her in any meaningful sense.

The smell of hospitals began to trigger something immediate and uncontrollable in him. A month after Priya's discharge, he had accompanied his wife to a routine appointment at their family physician's office. The moment he stepped through the door, the scent of disinfectant hit him—that same sharp, chemical smell from the ICU—and his chest tightened. His heart raced. He found himself unable to breathe normally, convinced with absolute certainty that something terrible was about to happen, that someone he loved was about to be taken from him. He left the office and sat in his car for forty minutes, sweating, his hands shaking too badly to drive.

Over the following months, he began to avoid situations involving medical settings. He stopped accompanying his wife to her appointments. He made excuses not to attend his nephew's school events, terrified that being around children would somehow trigger the memories of Priya's suffering, that he would lose control in front of them. At night, he found himself unable to sleep. Not tired—unable. His mind would not allow him to fully relax because some part of him remained convinced that if he let his guard down, if he stopped monitoring for danger, something catastrophic would happen. He would lie beside his wife, staring at the ceiling, his body tense, waiting for the next crisis.

The visual memories came without warning. He would be at work, reviewing equipment, and suddenly he would see the image of Priya's face contorted in pain during the spinal tap. The memory would arrive not as a thought but as a complete sensory experience—he could smell the hospital, feel the helplessness, hear her crying. These episodes were becoming more frequent. At work, his concentration had fractured. Three months ago, he had made an error during a routine inspection—a small one, caught by his supervisor before it became dangerous—but the error itself terrified him. He had come to believe that he was losing his mind, that his reactions since that week in the hospital meant something was fundamentally broken in him. He began to see himself differently: not as the careful, controlled man who had spent three decades mastering fear, but as someone weak and fundamentally helpless in the face of what life could do to him.

It was his wife, Meera, who finally insisted he seek help. She had noticed that he was withdrawing from their grandchildren's visits, that he had stopped going to work functions, that the man she had married was disappearing into something she could not reach. Rajesh came to the first appointment convinced that talking about it would only make him weaker, but he was also terrified that his deterioration would cost him everything—his career, his family, his sense of who he was. What he feared most was that the helplessness he had felt in that hospital room was not temporary. What he hoped for, though he barely dared to say it, was that he might find his way back to being the man he had been before Priya's illness—the man who could face danger without breaking. But he was no longer certain that man existed.
